newsitem.title: USA: Unions emphasize women in new recruiting drive.
newsitem.headline: Unions emphasize women in new recruiting drive.

text.p: America's union leaders on Monday unveiled ambitious plans to recruit more members, targeting women workers in particular, and to boost the struggling labour movement's sagging image.
John Sweeney, president of the AFL-CIO, said union membership was declining as a percentage of the work force and "unless we first put an emphasis on growth, none of our other strategies will work."

Sweeney, speaking at the annual winter meeting of the executive council of the American Federation of Labour and Congress of Industrial Organisations in Los Angeles, would not put a dollar figure on the sweeping initiative. But other union leaders said the AFL-CIO was committed to spending 30 percent of the $5 billion in annual income its unions received from members and other sources, or about $1.5 billion a year, on the recruiting drive.

The federation, an umbrella group of 78 affiliate unions, was meeting for the first time in more than 70 years outside its normal winter venue of the Florida coastal resort town of Bal Harbour in an effort to show its commitment to members nationwide.
It intends to hold future meetings in other urban settings. Los Angeles, with its large immigrant population, is known as the capital of America's low-wage work force.

The AFL-CIO is also committed to a $60 million advertising blitz to refurbish its image, as well as devoting $2 million to its two biggest current recruiting drives; the organising of 20,000 strawberry pickers in California, most of whom are immigrant workers, and continuing the successful unionizing of hotel and construction workers in Las Vegas.

In addressing reporters at a news briefing, Sweeney said the federation "hasn't listened enough to the concerns of working women and we haven't responded adequately to their needs. Our new campaign, 'Working Women Organise,' addresses those concerns and puts us on the right road."

Linda Chavez-Thompson, executive vice-president of the AFL-CIO, told reporters women voters made a big difference in the 1996 political elections and could make the same difference in the labour movement.
"Polls have statistically shown that women are more likely to join together with others to solve their problems than men are," she said.
Chavez-Thompson said that in 1960 women made up only 18 percent of union membership, while in 1972 the number had grown to 22 percent, increasing by 1996 to 39 percent.

Gloria Johnson, president of the Coalition of Labour Union Women and vice president of the executive council, said female union members earned an average of 38 percent more than non-union female workers and got 35 percent higher benefits.
In addition, the unions also addressed other concerns of working women, such as child care, flexible work schedules, workplace safety and retirement security, she said.
The person in charge of the new drive to bring more women into the union ranks is Karen Nussbaum, director of the Working Women's Department of the AFL-CIO, who outlined the campaign.

She said the federation would conduct an "Ask a Working Woman" survey "targeting women in every occupation, every walk of life in every part of the country to start a national dialogue about issues that working women care about the most." Nussbaum added that more than a million women would receive questionaires as part of the survey.

In addition, the federation intended to build partnerships with women's civil rights groups and community organisations around the country and there would be a 20-city tour by union organisers culminating in a conference for working women in Washington soon after Labour Day, she said.

The 54-member executive council was due to be addressed on Tuesday by Vice President Al Gore and House of Representatives minority leader Richard Gephardt, both seen as likely rivals for the Democratic presidential nomination in 2000.

While the federation's union membership drive is seen as ambitious, labour experts say it is an uphill battle. The number of union members nationwide dropped by 92,000 last year and by 338,000 the year before, according to national statistics.

The percentage of union members in the work force has dropped to 14.5 percent, compared with 35 percent in the 1950s, and with the work force growing at about two million a year, unions would have to recruit about 400,000 members annually just to keep pace, according to experts.
